https://www.barrons.com/articles/obsession-with-an-apple-car-is-not-dead-1530223079 Obsession With an Apple Car Is Not Dead By Updated June 28, 2018 5:57 p.m. ET Text Size Tiernan Ray Updated June 28, 2018 5:57 p.m. ET
It seems rumors of Apple ( AAPL ) making its own automobile haven’t been as prevalent of late, but not everyone has given up on the notion.
Rob Cihra of Guggenheim Securities , who rates Apple stock a Buy, with a $215 price target, writes that the company needs “big TAMs,” or “total addressable markets,” to keep its stock rising, and he expects the company “ultimately launches a self-driving CAR." Illustration of potential Apple Car. Illustration: Tiernan Ray for Barron's
His proposition is relatively simple: "Cars are complex PRODUCTS and Apple is a PRODUCT company, particularly good at engineering the integration of hardware + software."
He holds that belief despite “contrary news flow.”
Cihra notes that most people no longer think much will come of what was reported at one time to be a “ Project Titan ” at Apple to make a car, but he thinks the doubters are wrong just given how much the car mark matches Apple’s historical ambition:
We think consensus is that Apple has pulled back on ambitions to launch a car and is now just focusing on autonomous tech to sell to others, but we see no history of Apple acting as a “supplier” of core tech to other OEMs, and its entire business model rather built on owning/controlling the end-to-end experience. Although Apple has seemed a bit noncommittal to Project Titan since 2014, we believe it is nonetheless currently testing autonomous vehicles (one of 56 companies we count holding such permits with the California DMV) and we have seen Apple file patents so far in autonomous vehicle control, guidance and navigation systems, as well as related neural networking, AR, LiDAR detection, camera and machine vision systems; but also patents in specific areas including vehicle climate control and body structure. Given the market’s sheer size and parallels to Apple’s historical MO, we remain convinced that it will inevitably be drawn into launching its own car.
Of course, Apple’s services business is now its big growth driver, at $36 billion in calendar 2018 revenue, he projects. But the services biz is “still largely dependent on an installed base” of devices—it doesn’t help sell devices as much as it exploits them.
And content , with the recent announcement of the deal with Oprah Winfrey , is important, but really doesn’t “leverage either hardware or software engineering, which are Apple’s two primary strengths."
Instead, he likes the automotive market, “where a TAM of >$2 trillion is not only BIG enough to move the needle for Apple, but the 'cream-off-the-top' Luxury/Premium segment is >$400B alone, and where technology disruption is already coming from electrification + software + Transportation-as-a-Service (TaaS)."
To top it off, Apple has the AI and machine learning knowledge to make it work, he writes.
A lot of work is in the Cloud (e.g., Siri) but we believe Apple’s particular strengths are rather in EDGE computing for on-board AI/ML (e.g., A-series processor with Neural Engine, Face ID, Core ML for on-device inference). Apple recently hired away another high-profile AI engineer from Alphabet ( GOOG ), Jaime Waydo, lead systems engineer for Google’s Waymo self-driving cars; and, we see the move following, not coincidentally, its April hiring of Google’s former SVP Engineering, John Giannandrea, to become Apple’s new overall chief of machine learning and AI strategy.
Among the myriad considerations Cihra offers is that CEO Tim Cook could "leave his mark" by making Apple a " manufacturing company again ," especially given his historical expertise in supply chain.
And remember, he writes, automobiles are the " quintessential edge computer ," referring to the craze over computing at the edge of networks as opposed to data centers.
Apple shares today closed at $185.50, up $1.34, or 0.7%.
